title: The Economy’s Pulse
kicker: S&P Global / HSBC India PMI · to October 2026
lead: The Purchasing Managers' Index is the earliest monthly read on the economy — a survey of hundreds of firms on output, new orders, hiring and prices, out in the first days of each month — manufacturing on the first business day, services a few business days later — weeks before the official data. The rule is simple: above 50 means activity is expanding, below 50 means it is shrinking . This tracks the manufacturing and services PMIs month by month. India's manufacturing and services PMIs have both run above 50 for more than five years , every month since August 2021 — even as the pace waxes and wanes. S&P Global / HSBC data.
desc: The Purchasing Managers’ Index is the earliest monthly read on the economy — a survey of firms out weeks before the official data. Above 50 means growth, below 50 means contraction.
notes: What you're looking at. The PMI is a diffusion index : each month S&P Global asks purchasing managers whether activity is higher, the same, or lower than the month before, and scores the answers so that 50 is the no-change line . A reading of 55 means solidly more firms are growing than shrinking; 48 means the reverse. It is a breadth gauge, not a volume one — it tells you how widespread growth is, not by how much output rose. Because it is survey-based and out first, it leads IIP and GDP by weeks. The manufacturing and services indices are separate surveys; a composite blends the two. Figures are the final (not flash) monthly prints — the flash estimate, out about a week before month-end, is often revised (e.g. December 2024 manufacturing: flash 57.4, final 56.4).
source: Source: S&P Global / HSBC India Manufacturing & Services PMI — monthly, seasonally adjusted, final prints · PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta

title: The Cost Of Living
lead: This is the number that sets your EMIs. CPI-Combined is the inflation the RBI targets at 4%, within a 2–6% band — it decides whether interest rates, and your loan costs, rise or fall. Track the headline against that band, then drill into what's actually moving it: food, fuel, and the food basket right down to fruits and vegetables . Numbers are MoSPI's own , to the month.
desc: The one number that touches every household — and sets your EMIs. CPI-Combined is what the RBI targets at 4%, deciding whether rates and loan costs rise or fall.
notes: Reading the numbers. "Inflation" here is the year-on-year change in the price index — how much higher prices are than the same month a year earlier. It is not the same as prices themselves, which the index (a separate toggle) tracks. A number falling from, say, 6% to 3% means prices are still rising, just more slowly (disinflation); only a reading below zero means prices actually fell (deflation, which food items like vegetables and pulses do reach). The RBI's 2–6% tolerance band shown behind the chart is a target for the headline CPI-Combined only — it is not a target for Rural, Urban or any single category, so it appears only on the headline line. Headline inflation (Rural, Urban, Combined) uses MoSPI's published rate, final where a final figure exists: on the 2024=100 base from January 2026, and the official rate published on the 2012=100 base for 2014–2025 (MoSPI publishes no 2024-base rates for earlier months; there is none for 2013); sub-group inflation is the 12-month change computed from MoSPI's published index (validated to within 0.2 points of the official rate). Recent months are provisional and revised by MoSPI. Year-on-year readings carry base effects — an unusual month a year earlier can swing the current number. Source: MoSPI eSankhyiki .
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: The Nation’s Cash Register
lead: GST is the closest thing India has to a monthly pulse-check on its economy. It is the country's single largest source of indirect-tax revenue, and because almost every sale in the formal economy passes through it, the monthly collection moves with consumption, trade and the steady pull of businesses into the tax net — landing weeks ahead of GDP and most official growth data.
desc: Almost every formal sale is taxed once, right here. That makes GST the broadest live gauge of demand India has — when collections climb, tills are ringing from metros to mandis.
notes: Reading the numbers. "Domestic" is GST on home transactions; "Imports" is GST on imported goods — together they make the gross. The "12-month total" is a rolling sum of the trailing twelve months, which strips out GST's strong seasonality (April, on year-end sales, is always the peak — so GST rises year-on-year, not month-on-month). Coverage: all three national series reach back to August 2017 (GST launched 1 July 2017; the first returns were filed from August). For August 2017–March 2020 the gross figure is the government's monthly press-release total, and imports for those months are shown as gross minus the domestic collection. The by-state view is domestic only (imports are central, not state-attributable), runs through October 2026 , and overlays up to six states — use the range presets or Custom to set any window. State figures and cess: GSTN's state numbers include compensation cess up to March 2025 and exclude it from April 2025 (earlier than the national headline), so state levels step down at April 2025 (marked). State growth compares like with like: for April–October 2025 it uses the state table in each GSTN monthly report, where both years include cess; for November 2025–March 2026 GSTN published no state-wise monthly figures on a common basis, so state YoY is left blank there (shaded), as is the 12-month YoY from November 2025. From April 2026 both years exclude cess. May 2025 includes a one-time ~₹10,000 crore telecom-spectrum payment. Compensation cess. Up to October 2025 the gross includes compensation cess (roughly ₹12,000–13,000 crore a month); from November 2025 , after GST 2.0, the government's headline leaves it out, so the line steps down there (marked on the chart). Year-on-year growth is the official rate: from November 2025 each month is compared with the year-ago month also excluding cess , as printed in the same release, and the fiscal-year pace does the same. Comparing two levels on either side of the break by hand mixes the two bases.
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: A Billion Taps A Day
lead: Every month India has run on UPI — the value that moved, the number of payments, and what each works out to per day. Toggle value against volume, zoom into any stretch, and compare any two months or any two periods. Numbers are NPCI's own , to the month.
desc: India runs on UPI. Nearly every formal payment — a chai, a salary, a flat — passes through it, so the monthly value is the fastest read on whether the country is spending.
notes: Reading the numbers. NPCI notes this data excludes transactions with a debit and credit to the same account from August 2018 onwards , so figures on either side of that line aren't strictly like-for-like. April–June 2016 show near-zero volume: UPI was live at a handful of banks but had barely launched. "Average ticket" is value ÷ volume — the size of the typical payment. "Daily average" divides each month's figure by that month's number of days.
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: India’s Dollar War Chest
kicker: Weekly pulse · Reserve Bank of India
lead: Foreign-exchange reserves are India's financial shock-absorber — the war-chest the Reserve Bank draws on to steady the rupee, keep paying for imports when foreign money turns tail, and reassure markets that the country can always meet its external bills. They are reported every Friday, which makes them one of the most closely-watched weekly numbers in the economy.
desc: Reserves are what the rupee leans on when markets turn — how long the RBI can defend the currency, pay for imports and ride out a shock. Published every single week.
notes: Reading the numbers. The total is the sum of four parts: foreign-currency assets (dollars, euros, yen and other currencies the RBI holds, by far the largest share); gold ; SDRs , the reserve asset issued by the IMF; and the reserve tranche position , India's automatic-draw quota at the IMF. Reserves are a stock — a level on a given Friday, not a monthly flow — so a comparison shows the change between two dates. The SDR line jumps in August 2021 , when the IMF made a one-off general allocation of SDRs to all members. Figures are the RBI's US-dollar values; the reserves are also reported in rupees, shown in the tooltip for the total.
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: Money In, Money Out
kicker: Monthly pulse · Reserve Bank of India
lead: Bank credit and deposits are the clearest monthly read on India's banking system — how fast banks are lending, how fast money is flowing in, and the gap between the two. Switch between bank credit , aggregate deposits , and the credit–deposit ratio ; read the level in ₹ lakh crore or the year-on-year growth. Numbers are the RBI's own , to the month.
desc: Bank credit is how fast India is borrowing; deposits are how fast it’s saving. Credit leads investment and consumption, turning before GDP.
notes: Reading the numbers. "Growth" is the year-on-year change in outstanding on the last reporting date of the month. Bank credit leads investment and consumption, so it turns weeks-to-months before GDP. Deposits fund that lending; when credit grows faster than deposits, the credit–deposit ratio climbs — a sign banks are stretching their books (about 80% in August 2026, after a 2026 peak near 83% — high by the standard of the years since 2018). The step-up around July 2023 is the HDFC Ltd–HDFC Bank merger, which moved a large housing-loan book onto bank balance sheets overnight and inflates credit growth through mid-2024; it is a definitional shift, not a lending surge. By sector, RBI's latest release (fortnight ended 31 August 2026) shows non-food credit up 18.8% year-on-year, led by services ( 24.3% ), with industry at 18.2% , agriculture 17.2% and personal loans 16.9% ( RBI, Sectoral Deployment of Bank Credit – August 2026 ). The latest month is provisional and revised later. Source: RBI DBIE .
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: The Factory Floor
lead: The Index of Industrial Production is India's broadest monthly read on the factory floor — how much the country actually made, across mining, manufacturing and power. Split it two ways: by sector (mining, manufacturing, electricity) or by what the goods are for — primary, capital, intermediate, infrastructure, and consumer durables vs non-durables . Track the headline, then open up any strand. Numbers are MoSPI's own , to the month.
desc: The broadest monthly read on how much India actually makes — mining, manufacturing and power. Split it by sector, or by what the goods are for.
notes: Reading the numbers. "Growth" here is the year-on-year change in the output index — how much more (or less) India produced than in the same month a year earlier. It is volume of production, not price. Manufacturing dominates the General index (76.1% weight on the 2022–23 base; 77.6% on 2011–12), so the two move closely; the sectoral and use-based cuts show what is driving it. The eight core industries (a separate Pulse tool) are about 40% of the IIP and lead it by a few weeks. The index is not seasonally adjusted — March is a year-end peak — so read growth year-on-year. The April 2020 cliff is the COVID lockdown: capital goods fell to an index of 7 and consumer durables to 5.5, from about 100. The latest month is a Quick Estimate and is revised to final a month later; all earlier months are final. Base year: MoSPI retired the 2011–12 base at March 2026 and moved to a new 2022–23 base from April 2026. Both are offered here via the Base-year switch; index levels are not comparable across bases (March 2026 is 173.2 on the 2011–12 base and 129.7 on the 2022–23 base), and because the weights differ, growth for an overlapping month can differ modestly — e.g. March 2026 is +4.1% on the 2011–12 base and +3.0% on the 2022–23 base. Both are official. Source: MoSPI eSankhyiki .
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: The Engine Room
kicker: Monthly pulse · Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT
lead: Before GDP, before the broad factory-output numbers, nine industries tell you how India's engine room is running — coal, crude oil, natural gas, refining, fertilizers, steel , cement, electricity and, since the 2022–23 revision, iron ore. Together they are the infrastructure backbone and about a third of all industrial output (32.9% of the IIP's weight). Track the headline, then open up any single industry. Numbers are the Economic Adviser's own , to the month.
desc: Eight industries — coal, oil, gas, refining, fertilizers, steel, cement and power — form the infrastructure spine and about two-fifths of factory output.
notes: Reading the numbers. "Growth" here is the year-on-year change in the output index — how much more (or less) these industries produced than in the same month a year earlier. It is not the price of anything; it is volume of production. The core industries carry about a third (32.9%) of the weight of the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) on the 2022–23 base (about 40% on the old 2011–12 base), so they lead the broader factory-output story by a few weeks. The index is not seasonally adjusted : March is always a year-end production peak and April drops back, so the raw index (a separate toggle) is jagged — read growth year-on-year. The deep trough of April–May 2020 (on the 2011–12 series) is the COVID lockdown: in April 2020 steel output fell 82.8% and cement 85.2% year-on-year, and in May the falls narrowed to 40.4% and 21.4%. The latest month is provisional (shown dashed) and is revised in the next release, then frozen. Base change: OEA moved the index to base 2022–23 on 20 July 2026, adding iron ore, using gross (not net) steel output and only raw coal; the two bases are separate official series and are not spliced here. Source: Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT .
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: The Gap With The World
lead: Every month India ships goods out and buys goods in, and the gap between the two — the trade deficit — is one of the clearest reads on how the economy sits against the rest of the world. Exports show demand for what India makes; imports track appetite at home, and lean heavily on crude oil and gold.
desc: Every month India buys far more than it sells, and the gap is settled in dollars. Because imports ride on crude and gold, the deficit swings with global prices.
notes: Reading it. The red line is India's goods balance — deep in deficit. The green band is the services surplus (IT, software, business services) that fills most of that gap, leaving the blue net line: India's true trade balance with the world. Annual figures run through FY2024-25; from April 2025 the view switches to monthly. Goods are DGCIS (customs) data; services are RBI estimates, provisional for the latest months and revised with the quarterly balance of payments. Source: Ministry of Commerce & RBI.

Reading the numbers. This is merchandise (goods) trade only — it does not include services, where India runs a large surplus that offsets much of the goods deficit. The trade deficit is imports minus exports; India has run one in every month here except June 2020, when the lockdown briefly produced a small surplus. Imports are dominated by crude oil and gold , so the deficit swings with global oil prices. The 12-month view sums the trailing twelve months, which strips out the strong seasonality (exports typically peak in March, at the financial-year close). April 2020 is the COVID collapse, when both exports and imports fell about 60% from a year earlier.
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: The Trade Ledger
lead: Every dollar and rupee India exports and imports — split into oil and everything else, and the gap between the two — going back to 1986-87. Switch the currency and watch how much of the "growth" is really the rupee sliding against the dollar.
desc: India’s exports and imports since 1986 — oil and everything else, in dollars and rupees, and the deficit between them. Flip currency to separate growth from rupee drift.
notes: India’s exports and imports since 1986 — oil and everything else, in dollars and rupees, and the deficit between them. Flip currency to separate growth from rupee drift.

title: The Price Of A Dollar
kicker: Rupee vs Dollar · High Frequency Pulse
lead: How many rupees it takes to buy one US dollar — the single most watched number in India's external economy. Track it three ways: the monthly average back to 1973, the weekly Wednesday close since 2004, and the daily close, kept live to the latest session. Rates are FRED's own .
desc: The rupee’s price against the dollar sets the cost of everything India buys abroad — oil, gold, chips, a degree overseas. Pegged near ₹8 in 1973 to past ₹85 today.
notes: The rupee’s price against the dollar sets the cost of everything India buys abroad — oil, gold, chips, a degree overseas. Pegged near ₹8 in 1973 to past ₹85 today.
All data compiled and updated directly from the primary issuing authority.
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: The Price Of Borrowing
lead: The yield on the 10-year government bond — what it costs the Centre to borrow for a decade, and the benchmark that quietly sets the price of money for everyone else, from home loans to company debt. When it climbs, the government's interest bill and your EMIs feel it. Toggle the monthly average back to 2011, or the daily benchmark for the past year. OECD & FBIL data.
desc: The yield on the 10-year government bond is the price the Centre pays to borrow — and the benchmark that quietly sets every other rate, from home loans to corporate bonds.
notes: Reading the yield. This is the return an investor earns holding a 10-year Government of India bond to maturity — and because that debt is effectively risk-free, its yield is the benchmark off which almost every other interest rate in the country is priced. It rises when inflation or borrowing is expected to climb, or when the RBI tightens, and falls when growth worries or rate cuts loom — note the plunge to 5.8% in the COVID summer of 2020 and the nearly 9% peak during the 2013–14 taper tantrum. The monthly line is the OECD's benchmark average (via FRED) since 2011, now through September 2026 (FBIL's own monthly average has stayed within 2.5 basis points of the OECD's in the months both are available); the daily view is FBIL's published 10-year par yield. Latest reading: 18 September 2026 .
source: Source: OECD Main Economic Indicators — Long-Term (10-Year Benchmark) Government Bond Yield for India, compiled from RBI/FBIL · monthly average · PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta

title: Prices At The Source
kicker: Monthly pulse · Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT
lead: Before prices reach the shop shelf, they move at the wholesale level — and the Wholesale Price Index is where India reads that first. It carries no consumer-style target band; instead it tracks the raw cost of goods across the economy, weighted heavily toward manufactured products , with fuel & power the most volatile piece. Track the headline, then split it into primary articles, fuel, factory goods and food. Numbers are the Economic Adviser's own , to the month.
desc: Before prices reach the shelf, they move at the wholesale level — and the WPI reads them first. Weighted toward factory goods and driven at the margin by fuel.
notes: Reading the numbers. "Inflation" here is the year-on-year change in the wholesale price index — how much higher wholesale prices are than the same month a year earlier. It is not the same as prices themselves, which the index (a separate toggle) tracks. A number falling from, say, 6% to 3% means wholesale prices are still rising, just more slowly (disinflation); only a reading below zero means they actually fell (deflation, which WPI reached from late 2014 through mid-2016, briefly in April–July 2020, in mid-2023, and again in several months of 2025). Unlike CPI, WPI has no RBI target band — it is a cost gauge, not a policy target, though it feeds into GDP deflators and input-cost pressure. All Commodities is a weighted average of Primary Articles, Fuel & Power and Manufactured Products (weights 22.76 / 14.11 / 63.13 on the 2022–23 base; 22.62 / 13.15 / 64.23 on the old 2011–12 base); the Food Index cuts across primary and manufactured food. The latest two months are provisional (shown dashed) and are revised in later monthly releases. On the discontinued 2011–12 base, March and April 2026 remain provisional: no OEA release with final old-base figures for them could be located, and the values shown are those in its last old-base index file (monthly_index_202606.xls), which differ slightly from the April 2026 press print (e.g. All Commodities April 167.6 vs 167.0). Source: Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT .
© PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta
source: Official Government of India & Regulatory Releases · India, in Numbers

title: What India Runs On
lead: Every month the country burns close to 20 million tonnes of petroleum products — diesel in trucks and tractors, petrol in cars and two-wheelers, LPG in kitchens, jet fuel in the sky. This tracks all twelve products, month by month, back to 1998 : the boom years, the COVID collapse, and the slow death of kerosene. Pick a fuel and watch it move.
desc: Every month India burns close to 20 million tonnes of petroleum — diesel in trucks, petrol in cars, LPG in kitchens, jet fuel in the sky. Track all twelve fuels since 1998.
notes: Every month India burns close to 20 million tonnes of petroleum — diesel in trucks, petrol in cars, LPG in kitchens, jet fuel in the sky. Track all twelve fuels since 1998.
All data compiled and updated directly from the primary issuing authority.
source: Polity Policy.com by Tushar Gupta · India, in Numbers — No Rhetoric, Just Data

title: Keeping The Lights On
lead: How much electricity India's power stations actually generate each month — and the fuel mix behind it. This tracks conventional generation : the coal and gas plants, big hydro dams, nuclear reactors and imports that the grid dispatches on demand. Watch coal do the heavy lifting, hydro swell every monsoon, and total output climb with the economy. CEA / National Power Portal data. Excludes solar and wind, which are metered separately.
desc: How much electricity India’s power stations generate every month — and the fuel mix behind it. Watch coal and gas do heavy lifting, hydro swell in monsoon, and thermal PLF.
notes: What you're looking at. Each bar of the stack is a fuel source's output for the month, in billion units (BU — one unit is a kilowatt-hour); the top of the stack is total conventional generation. Coal and gas ("thermal") supply roughly four-fifths of it and set the baseline; hydro is the seasonal wave that fills every monsoon and thins out by winter; nuclear is the steady sliver; imports are mostly hydropower from Bhutan. The coal-utilisation view shows thermal plant load factor — the share of their rated capacity that coal and lignite stations actually run at (CEA computes it for coal/lignite plants only, not gas) — which has risen from barely half in 2019–20 (a low of 42% in the April 2020 lockdown) to roughly 65–75% in recent years, peaking at about 76% in April 2024. Figures are CEA's monthly generation report, using CEA's actual load factor (not its programme target); the most recent month is provisional (CEA's tentative report) until CEA publishes the actual. This series does not include solar, wind or small-hydro (renewable) generation, which CEA reports under a separate account.
source: Source: Central Electricity Authority — Monthly Generation Report , via the National Power Portal · conventional generation (thermal, nuclear, hydro & imports), excludes renewables · PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta

title: What The Nation Hauls
lead: Every year Indian Railways moves the raw material of the economy — coal to power plants, ore and limestone to steel and cement works, fertiliser to farms, containers to ports. This tracks freight loading : the total originating tonnage the network carries each financial year, and the commodities that make it up. Watch the tonnage climb from about 1,209 MT in FY2019-20 to a record 1,670 MT — and see how far coal still dominates the load. Ministry of Railways data.
desc: Indian Railways moves the raw material of the economy — coal to power plants, ore to steel mills, fertiliser to farms, containers to ports. Record 1,600+ MT annually.
notes: What you're looking at. "Freight loading" is the originating tonnage Indian Railways carries — counted once, where each consignment starts — in million tonnes (MT) per financial year (April–March). It is the headline the Ministry reports each year and a clean read on the goods economy: coal for power, ore and fluxes for steel, cement, fertiliser, foodgrains and containerised trade all ride the rails. Coal alone is about half the load, which is why railway freight tracks power demand so closely. The What it carries view breaks the latest year down by commodity. Annual figures are the Ministry's headline originating loading as first published in its year-end statement; monthly figures are the Ministry's first-published monthly numbers. Commodity tonnages are shown only where the Ministry has published them. Freight loading counts tonnes originating, not tonne-kilometres, so it does not capture how far each consignment travels.
source: Source: Ministry of Railways — freight loading (originating tonnage); every year is the Ministry's headline loading as first published in its year-end statement (via PIB ); months from the Ministry's monthly freight releases · PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta

title: What The Nation Ships
kicker: Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways · to October 2026
lead: India's major ports — the twelve big public gateways from Deendayal and Paradip to JNPA and Visakhapatnam — handle the bulk of the country's seaborne trade: crude and POL, coal, containers, iron ore, fertiliser and more. This tracks the cargo they move , month by month, and how it splits port by port. Traffic reached a record 915 MT in FY2025-26, up about 7% , and the monthly run has stayed strong into FY2026-27. Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways data.
desc: India’s twelve big public ports handle most of the country’s seaborne trade — crude, coal, containers, iron ore. Month by month throughput across Deendayal, Paradip, JNPA.
notes: What you're looking at. India has twelve major ports — the big public ports run under the central government (Deendayal, Paradip, JNPA, Visakhapatnam, Mumbai, Chennai and others). They handle a little over half of the country's total seaborne cargo; the rest goes through state and private "non-major" ports such as Mundra and Adani's network. This tracks the cargo traffic at the major ports in million tonnes (MT): the Cargo handled view is month by month, the Port by port view splits the latest full year across the twelve. Figures are the Ministry's monthly reports, each month taken as printed in its own report; together they match the official cumulatives and the 914.7 MT year total to within rounding. Cargo traffic counts tonnes handled (loaded plus unloaded), so it is not directly comparable to railway freight loading, which counts originating tonnes only.
source: Source: Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways — monthly "Cargo handled at Major Ports" reports and the Indian Ports Association · PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta

title: The Nation On Wheels
lead: How many vehicles Indians actually drove home each month — two-wheelers, cars, tractors, trucks and more — from FADA 's retail registration data, sourced from the government's VAHAN portal. Retail is what left the showroom, not what makers shipped to dealers.
desc: Every month millions of Indians take delivery of a new vehicle — a scooter, a hatchback, a tractor, a truck. Retail registrations from FADA VAHAN portal.
notes: Reading the numbers. These are retail sales — vehicles registered at RTOs when a buyer takes delivery — not wholesale dispatches to dealers. FADA compiles them from the Ministry of Road Transport's VAHAN portal (~1,460 of ~1,470 RTOs). The recurring October–November peaks are the festive season; October 2025 is amplified by the September 2025 GST 2.0 rate cut, which pulled buyers off the fence — note the matching September dip. The Total follows FADA's headline. Each point is the month's figure as first published in that month's FADA release. The year-on-year growth is FADA's own: this month's count against the year-ago month as FADA reprints it in the same release. FADA keeps back-dating registrations to VAHAN for weeks, so that year-ago figure is usually a few percent higher than the one first published a year earlier. That is why a month's growth can't always be read off the two points on the chart. Construction equipment sat inside Commercial Vehicles until April 2025 and has been its own category since May 2025, so the Commercial Vehicles line steps down slightly there; FADA restated the year-ago figures, so the growth rates are unaffected. The fiscal-year-to-date figure is FADA's own cumulative table.
source: Source: FADA monthly Vehicle Retail Data (VAHAN) · FY24–FY27 · PolityPolicy · India, in Numbers · by Tushar Gupta

title: The Bad-Loan Decade
lead: A decade ago India's banks were drowning in loans that would never be repaid — the "twin balance-sheet" crisis. Bad loans climbed from a few percent to a peak near one rupee in nine lent out, then were written down, provisioned and recovered. Pick a bank group and watch the rise and the cleanup.

title: India’s Harvest
lead: Since 1968 India has gone from feeding itself on the brink to a foodgrain surplus — and it did it almost entirely on the same land . Pick a crop and see it three ways: how much was grown, how much land it took, and the yield squeezed from each hectare. Flip from foodgrains to the commercial crops — sugarcane, cotton, tea, coffee — to see where the cash economy grew.
